7.translation: For all embodied beings He is within and without: within as the Puruṣa, and without in the forms of Time; the plural is with reference to the divisions of Time. He bestows death and immortality. For those whose vision is inward, He gives liberation as the Inner Controller; for those whose vision is outward, He gives death in the form of Time.

15.translation: “Vyavasitā” means firmly resolved, having made a definite determination. “Yat” has the sense of “because,” with reference to that settled understanding.

18.translation: Having approached, she stood in the presence of the mighty one.

21.translation: “Pauruṣī” means belonging to the Puruṣa, Bhagavān: “Hear that speech from me at once. Do not delay. Let it be carried out exactly so.”

22.translation: Even before the petition was made, the Puruṣa, the Lord, had perceived and ascertained the distress.

27.translation: For the Lord’s descent in the prison of the Bhoja king, the introductory narrative begins with the verse “Śūrasena” and continues to the end of the chapter. “Mathurām āvasan” means dwelling in Mathurā; “viṣayān” means regions or lands.

29.translation: “Sūryayā” is glossed as “with the newly wedded woman”; “prayāṇe” means “for departure.”

30.translation: “Raśmīn” means the reins; “pragṛhān” means the reins held in the hand.

31.translation: “Pāribarham” means accompanying equipment or bridal gifts; “upaskaram” means equipment or paraphernalia.

34.translation: “Ābhāṣya” means “having addressed,” as in “Ho, Kaṃsa!” “Hantā” means “killer”; “haniṣyati,” “he will kill.”

35.translation: “Kula-pāṃsana” means a disgrace to the family. “Ārabdha” means intent on acting or ready to act. “Kace” means by the hair, at the bound hair.

40.word_for_word: atra dṛṣṭāntaḥ — here is the example; vrajan — while moving; ekena agrataḥ nihitena padā tiṣṭhan — standing supported by one foot placed ahead; bhuvam avaṣṭabhya — bracing against the ground; deham bibhrat — supporting the body; paścāt anyena — afterward with the other foot; pūrva-pradeśāt utthāpya — lifting it from its former place; puraḥ nihitena gacchati — he goes forward by placing it ahead; tadvat — in the same way; tṛṇa-jalūkā — a leech on grass; tṛṇāntaram avaṣṭabhya — grasping another blade of grass; pūrvam tṛṇam tyajati — then lets go of the former blade; karma-pathe vartamānaḥ jīvaḥ api — so also a living being moving along the path of karma.
40.translation: The example is a person walking: supported on one foot placed ahead, he lifts the other from its former place and sets it forward. In the same way, a leech first grasps another blade of grass and then releases the former one. So too a living being proceeds on the path of karma.

42.translation: One may ask: since the karmas producing varied bodies have already been performed, what determines the attainment of a particular body? Among the five elements fashioned by māyā into many bodily forms, the mind, impelled by destiny—that is, by karma coming to fruition—runs toward whichever divine, animal, or other body it takes up. Through identification, the embodied being is born there. If one objects that, since the mind is the agent, only the mind should be born, “prapadyamānaḥ” means that the self identifies with it, thinking “that is I,” and is born together with it.

43.translation: One may say: although some future body will indeed arise, one might still do even what should not be done to preserve this especially dear royal body. The answer is the example of light. Light such as the moon, reflected in water-filled earthen vessels or in water, oil, or ghee, appears to tremble when the reflecting medium follows the movement of the wind. Likewise, the self enters bodies fashioned by its own ignorance under the influence of attachment and becomes deluded through identification with them. Through mutual superimposition, bodily qualities such as thinness appear in the self, while qualities of the self, such as being an object of love, are attributed to the body. Since there is no ultimate distinction between the body of a king and that of a boar, the attempt to counteract death is futile.

45.translation: He again uses conciliation. “Putrikopamā” means like a little girl or doll; “dāru-mayī iva,” as though made of wood; “acetana-prāyā,” almost inanimate.

47.translation: The name “Ānakadundubhi” carries the intention already indicated by the earlier expression “mahā-bhāga.” Having understood the situation, he adopted the forthcoming plan of handing over the offspring in order to counteract, remedy, or deceive.

49.translation: Therefore, to avoid the fault of neglect, I will act in this way: by handing over the sons to “death,” that is, to Kaṃsa. If one objects that even this is not just: if sons should be born to me from her, let whatever is destined happen; meanwhile life will at least continue. If this man himself should die in the interval, then there is no injustice.

54.translation: What the bodiless voice said, exactly as it said it, is certainly fixed. Your danger does not come from Devakī herself; it arises from her sons. Since it was said, “the eighth will kill you,” and “eighth” depends on relative counting, all of them could be eighth. Therefore I will hand over all her sons.

56.translation: “When the time came” means when the time of delivery arrived. “Sarva-devatā” means she whose deity is Bhagavān, the Self of all; alternatively, “sarva-devatā-mayī,” because she is the receptacle of Bhagavān.

58.translation: How could he hand his son over to death? “Sādhūnām” refers to truthful, righteous persons; “satya-sandhānām,” to those firmly committed to truth; “viduṣām,” to those who know that Bhagavān alone is the reality and nothing else; “kadaryāṇām,” to the base, for whom no improper act is impossible; and “dhṛtātmānām,” to those who hold Hari, the Self, firmly in the heart—for whom what is difficult to give up?

66.translation: “Nigaḍaiḥ” means “with fetters” or “with chains.” “Aja,” the Unborn, is Viṣṇu; “tat-śaṅkayā” means from suspicion or fear that He would appear.
